<section class="content-section pro-teaching" id="pro-l08-situation"><h2>One situation can produce several kinds of output</h2><p>You are about to start a race. You deliberately adjust your feet, while your heart rate rises and your mouth feels dry. These changes can happen together, but they do not all use the same kind of motor pathway. To classify a pathway, follow its destination: <strong>what receives the output?</strong></p><p>The PNS links the brain and spinal cord with receptors, muscles, glands, and internal organs. Sensory pathways carry information inward toward the CNS. Motor pathways carry commands outward. The familiar count is <strong>12 pairs of cranial nerves</strong> associated with the brain and <strong>31 pairs of spinal nerves</strong> associated with the spinal cord. Individual nerves may contain several kinds of fibres, so the name of one nerve does not mean that every fibre in it performs the same job.</p></section>
<section class="content-section pro-teaching" id="pro-l08-organization"><h2>Read the organization from location to function</h2>
<figure class="learning-figure" data-canvas-helper-edit-key="p3-chapter-606">
<a aria-label="Enlarge: Read down from nervous system to CNS and PNS, then follow the sensory and motor branches. The autonomic branch divides further into sympathetic and parasympathetic systems." class="figure-open" data-canvas-helper-edit-key="p3-chapter-607" data-preview-enlarge="" data-preview-image-id="ch11-embedded-image-14" href="#ch11-embedded-image-14" rel="noopener">
<img alt="Read down from nervous system to CNS and PNS, then follow the sensory and motor branches. The autonomic branch divides further into sympathetic and parasympathetic systems." data-canvas-helper-edit-key="p3-chapter-608" data-original-src="assets/source/chapter11-pns-0.svg" decoding="async" id="ch11-embedded-image-14" loading="lazy" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"/>
</a>
<figcaption>
<strong>Figure 13.</strong> Read down from nervous system to CNS and PNS, then follow the sensory and motor branches. The autonomic branch divides further into sympathetic and parasympathetic systems. </figcaption>
</figure>
<p>Begin with the first split. <strong>CNS versus PNS is a distinction about location.</strong> The brain and spinal cord are central; peripheral nerves connect them to the body. Next, follow the PNS branches by function: sensory information goes toward the CNS and motor output goes away.</p><p>Below motor output, the somatic branch leads to skeletal muscle. The autonomic branch leads to smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands. The connecting lines indicate “is part of” or “leads to this pathway”; they do not show a single impulse visiting every branch. The two lowest boxes, sympathetic and parasympathetic, are subdivisions of autonomic output.</p><p>The broader <strong>sensory-somatic system</strong> includes sensory information from the body and somatic motor output. That is why a description of the somatic system may mention both sensation and movement, while a motor-division chart places “somatic” on its output branch. Read what the chart is classifying.</p></section>
<section class="content-section pro-teaching" id="pro-l08-effectors"><h2>Distinguish somatic and autonomic control by their effectors</h2><p><strong>Somatic motor neurons</strong> activate skeletal muscles, such as the muscles that move your fingers and legs. Many such movements are voluntary, but skeletal muscles also participate in reflexes. A knee-jerk response is involuntary and still uses somatic motor output.</p><p><strong>Autonomic motor pathways</strong> regulate smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands. Examples include changing the diameter of digestive-tract muscles, adjusting heart activity, and altering gland secretion. These pathways operate without requiring you to consciously set each organ's activity.</p><p>In a typical somatic motor route, one motor neuron runs from the CNS to skeletal muscle. A typical autonomic route uses a two-neuron chain, with a synapse in a peripheral <strong>ganglion</strong>, a cluster of neuron cell bodies outside the CNS. The first neuron is preganglionic and the second is postganglionic. This is a useful general organization; some pathways, including the adrenal medulla connection, are specialized.</p><h3>Worked classification: moving a foot while the heart speeds up</h3><ol class="pro-steps"><li><strong>Identify each effector separately.</strong> Foot movement uses skeletal muscle; the heart uses cardiac muscle.</li><li><strong>Classify the outgoing routes.</strong> Output to the foot is somatic. Autonomic activity helps adjust heart rate.</li><li><strong>Explain why the setting does not settle the category.</strong> Both can occur during a race, but “exercise” is not a nervous-system division.</li><li><strong>Allow coordination.</strong> Sensory information and CNS processing influence both routes. The categories describe linked components, not isolated systems.</li></ol><p>Breathing also reminds us to distinguish levels: brainstem circuits help generate automatic breathing patterns, while motor output to the diaphragm reaches skeletal muscle. “It happens automatically” is not enough to classify every motor fibre as autonomic.</p></section>
<section class="content-section pro-practice" data-pro-formative="biology30-ch11:pro-evaluation:2026-10-03:v1:l08-guided" id="pro-evaluation-2026-10-03-v1-l08-guided"><h3>A reflex is not automatically autonomic</h3><p>A person's knee extends during a patellar reflex, and the pupils constrict in bright light. Classify the motor output in each response and justify the distinction using the effectors.</p><div class="pro-response"><label for="pro-evaluation-2026-10-03-v1-l08-guided-response">Your reasoning — optional practice space (not saved)</label><textarea aria-describedby="pro-evaluation-2026-10-03-v1-l08-guided-response-note" autocomplete="off" id="pro-evaluation-2026-10-03-v1-l08-guided-response" rows="4" spellcheck="true"></textarea><p class="muted" id="pro-evaluation-2026-10-03-v1-l08-guided-response-note">Try it before opening the model. Compare your own reasoning; this response is not automatically marked or included in chapter progress.</p></div><details><summary>Hint: involuntary describes both responses</summary><p>Which response acts on skeletal muscle, and which acts on smooth muscle in the iris?</p></details><details><summary>Compare your reasoning</summary><p>The knee reflex uses somatic motor output to skeletal muscle. Pupil constriction uses autonomic output to smooth muscle in the iris. Both responses are involuntary, so voluntary versus involuntary alone cannot make this distinction. Name the target tissue as your evidence.</p></details></section>
<section class="content-section pro-teaching" id="pro-l08-autonomic"><h2>Sympathetic activity redistributes effort</h2><p>The <strong><button aria-haspopup="dialog" class="bio-term" data-bio-term="sympathetic division" data-bio-term-route="lesson-08" type="button">sympathetic division</button></strong> contributes to a fight-or-flight response. The heart can beat faster, air passages widen, and the liver releases glucose. These changes support rapid activity by helping supply oxygen and fuel. At the same time, digestion and bladder emptying can be reduced. “Sympathetic” does not mean that every organ speeds up.</p><p>The <strong><button aria-haspopup="dialog" class="bio-term" data-bio-term="parasympathetic division" data-bio-term-route="lesson-08" type="button">parasympathetic division</button></strong> supports functions often described as rest and digest: the heart slows, digestion increases, and bladder emptying is promoted. These divisions often have opposing effects on the same organ, adjusting its activity as conditions change. They are not two switches with the entire body locked into only one at a time.</p>
<figure class="learning-figure" data-canvas-helper-edit-key="p3-chapter-628">
<a aria-label="Enlarge: Compare the two responses organ by organ. Use the textbook’s Figure 11.36 for the larger organ list required by review question 4." class="figure-open" data-canvas-helper-edit-key="p3-chapter-629" data-preview-enlarge="" data-preview-image-id="ch11-embedded-image-15" href="#ch11-embedded-image-15" rel="noopener">
<img alt="Compare the two responses organ by organ. Use the textbook’s Figure 11.36 for the larger organ list required by review question 4." data-canvas-helper-edit-key="p3-chapter-630" data-original-src="assets/source/chapter11-pns-1.svg" decoding="async" id="ch11-embedded-image-15" loading="lazy" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"/>
</a>
<figcaption>
<strong>Figure 14.</strong> Compare the two responses organ by organ. Use the textbook’s Figure 11.36 for the larger organ list required by review question 4. </figcaption>
</figure>
<p>Read one organ row across both columns before moving to the next. For the heart, compare rate increases with rate decreases. For digestion, the direction reverses. The visual therefore compares effects on the <em>same organ</em>, rather than treating “increase” as a property of an entire division.</p>
<div aria-label="Scrollable comparison table" class="pro-table-wrap" role="region" tabindex="0"><table><thead><tr><th>Structure</th><th>Sympathetic pattern during a stress response</th><th>Parasympathetic pattern or limit of the comparison</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Eyes: pupils</td><td>Dilate</td><td>Constrict</td></tr><tr><td>Salivary glands</td><td>Reduced watery salivation in the simplified stress response</td><td>Increased salivation</td></tr><tr><td>Bronchioles</td><td>Widening supports airflow</td><td>Constriction</td></tr><tr><td>Heart</td><td>Heart rate increases</td><td>Heart rate decreases</td></tr><tr><td>Liver</td><td>Glucose release supports fuel availability</td><td>Do not confuse the liver with the separately shown gallbladder, whose bile release supports digestion.</td></tr><tr><td>Adrenal medulla</td><td>Release of epinephrine and norepinephrine into blood</td><td>No matching direct parasympathetic pathway is shown in this model.</td></tr><tr><td>Kidneys</td><td>Reduced activity is included in the simplified stress model</td><td>No matching direct parasympathetic pathway is shown; avoid inventing an equal opposite.</td></tr><tr><td>Stomach</td><td>Digestive activity decreases</td><td>Digestive activity increases</td></tr><tr><td>Pancreas</td><td>Digestive activity is reduced in the comparison</td><td>Digestive secretion is promoted</td></tr><tr><td>Intestines</td><td>Movement and digestive activity decrease</td><td>Movement and digestive activity increase</td></tr><tr><td>Bladder</td><td>Urine storage is favoured; emptying is inhibited</td><td>Bladder emptying is promoted</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>This is a comparison of coordinated response patterns, not a claim that every organ receives an identical pair of opposing nerves. For example, heart rate and vascular resistance both influence blood pressure; it is too simple to call the parasympathetic division a direct opposite for every sympathetic blood-vessel effect.</p></section>
<section class="content-section pro-teaching" id="pro-l08-transmitters"><h2>Connect the pathways to their chemical messengers</h2>
<figure class="learning-figure" data-canvas-helper-edit-key="p3-chapter-631">
<a class="figure-open" data-canvas-helper-edit-key="p3-chapter-632" data-preview-enlarge="" data-preview-image-id="ch11-embedded-image-16" href="#ch11-embedded-image-16" rel="noopener">
<img alt="Figure 11.36, p. 398, retained for Section 11.3 review question 4. It shows the specific organ list and the source’s transmitter key." data-canvas-helper-edit-key="p3-chapter-633" data-original-src="assets/source/chapter11-pns-2.png" decoding="async" id="ch11-embedded-image-16" loading="lazy" src="data:image/webp;base64,"/>
</a>
<figcaption>Figure 11.36, p. 398, retained for Section 11.3 review question 4. It shows the specific organ list and the source’s transmitter key.</figcaption>
</figure>
<p>Use the transmitter key at the bottom of this larger diagram. The blue pathways use acetylcholine and the red pathways use norepinephrine. Those colours do not mean sensory versus motor, or simply excitatory versus inhibitory. The small ganglia mark synaptic relays outside the CNS.</p><p>Both autonomic divisions use ACh at their preganglionic synapses. Many sympathetic postganglionic neurons use norepinephrine; parasympathetic postganglionic neurons usually use ACh. There are exceptions, including sympathetic signalling to sweat glands. You need the main pattern without turning it into an absolute rule.</p><p>At the adrenal medulla, sympathetic input triggers release of epinephrine and norepinephrine into the bloodstream. In this setting they act as hormones and can influence distant target tissues. A hormone travelling in blood and a neurotransmitter released into a synaptic cleft use different delivery routes, even when a chemical name overlaps.</p>

<section class="content-section pro-practice" data-pro-formative="biology30-ch11:pro-evaluation:2026-10-03:v1:l08-independent" id="pro-evaluation-2026-10-03-v1-l08-independent"><h3>Predict recovery and evaluate the evidence</h3><p>Someone is waiting to give a presentation. Heart rate increases, the mouth feels dry, and digestion slows. Afterward, heart rate settles and digestion resumes. Explain the autonomic pattern before and after. A polygraph records the earlier changes: does that establish that the person was lying?</p><div class="pro-response"><label for="pro-evaluation-2026-10-03-v1-l08-independent-response">Your reasoning — optional practice space (not saved)</label><textarea aria-describedby="pro-evaluation-2026-10-03-v1-l08-independent-response-note" autocomplete="off" id="pro-evaluation-2026-10-03-v1-l08-independent-response" rows="4" spellcheck="true"></textarea><p class="muted" id="pro-evaluation-2026-10-03-v1-l08-independent-response-note">Try it before opening the model. Compare your own reasoning; this response is not automatically marked or included in chapter progress.</p></div><details><summary>Model and self-check</summary><p>The earlier pattern is consistent with increased sympathetic activity during perceived stress. As the challenge ends, reduced sympathetic drive and parasympathetic influence can support recovery, including slower heart rate and greater digestive activity. A polygraph measures physiological changes, not truthfulness directly. Anticipation, fear, exertion, and other causes can produce similar changes. Check that you linked three organ effects and distinguished the measurement from the claim about its cause.</p></details></section>
<section class="content-section pro-teaching"><p><strong>Carry forward:</strong> the PNS carries input and output through pathways with different targets. The next lesson returns to the CNS to explain its tissue organization, the spinal cord's two main jobs, and the protection of these structures.</p></section>
